sm: Joe Sternberg hosts this Potomac Watch with Kim Strassel and Barton Swain, on the leadership elections now under way in Washington. In the Senate, Chuck Schumer, Democratic leader since 2017, faces a challenge from Chris Van Hollen of Maryland even though Democrats just won 56 seats. Kim says the two differ little on policy, but Schumer has not backed Medicare for all or been as hostile to Israel as the party's left, and the challenge also serves as a warning. She notes Schumer has many allies and the vote is secret and not until December 1. Barton adds that Van Hollen once strongly supported Israel. A clip has Van Hollen calling for new leadership, and Joe notes Schumer is 75 and Van Hollen 67.

The hosts say the left wants big achievements but may find ideas like Medicare for all unpopular, and that the midterm was more a vote against President Trump than for Democrats. Barton laments the win of Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, which he says will embolden the left. He is more hopeful about a new group of Democratic senators from purple or red states, including Josh Turek, Annie Andrews, Scott Colom, Sherrod Brown, a Kansas Democrat and possibly Mary Peltola, who could resist ending the filibuster or expanding the Supreme Court. Kim says Bernie Sanders's reconciliation push is meant to pressure the 2028 nominee, but failing to pass it would be embarrassing. Joe then turns to what House Democrats under Hakeem Jeffries should do, with the base wanting impeachments and investigations.

Barton says the squad has grown from seven to about 16 members and now calls itself the block, and he would advise Hakeem Jeffries to promise nothing. Kim says moderate majority makers outnumber them and warns Democrats could repeat 2009 and 2010, when such members were made to vote for Obamacare and then lost. She suggests taking a popular issue, like Obamacare subsidies and health costs, and winning an incremental deal as Newt Gingrich did on welfare reform. Joe asks whether Democrats' base would accept any bill Trump signs. Kim says Trump is a deal maker and Democrats could lure him into deals, but she expects them to waste the chance. Barton says he has urged working with Trump since 2016.

Barton points to Hakeem Jeffries's harsh statement on Stephen Miller being named chief of staff, which he reads as a sign Jeffries will not stand behind Trump signing bills. He expects Democrats to waste two years on impeachment, investigations and performative politics. The hosts then turn to Republicans, where Jim Jordan of Ohio has won the House Republican leadership race and says 35 new Republicans are coming in. Kim sees reason for optimism after years of bitter leadership fights, and notes Jordan spent his career leading the Republican Study Committee and the Freedom Caucus on policy. Barton welcomes the departure of some rabble rousers and hopes Jordan can teach Republicans to explain policy, citing Medicaid reform as an example of poor explanation.
